title: Diode Rectifier Circuits: Half Wave and Full Wave Explained
text:
Electronics

 Diode Rectifier Circuits: Half Wave and Full Wave Explained

 A diode rectifier circuit converts AC voltage to pulsating DC by using the one-way conducting property of diodes. Half wave rectifiers use one diode and pass only one half of the AC cycle. Full wave rectifiers use two or four diodes and pass both halves.

 This guide covers all three diode rectifier types with waveforms, formulas, worked examples, and a live output voltage calculator.

 
 Half Wave 
 Full Wave Centre Tap 
 Bridge Rectifier 
 Ripple and Smoothing 
 




 A diode rectifier circuit produces pulsating DC. The average output voltage depends on the peak input voltage and the rectifier type: 0.318 × Vpeak for half wave, 0.636 × Vpeak for full wave. A filter capacitor smooths the ripple to usable DC.


 Diode Rectifier Circuit: How Diodes Convert AC to DC


 
 Hi everyone! Today we are going to look at diode rectifier circuits -- one of the most fundamental building blocks in power electronics. Every DC power supply, battery charger, and electronic device that runs from a mains plug contains a rectifier of one type or another. Let us go through the three main types: half wave, full wave centre tap, and full wave bridge.


 
 
 
 
 A diode conducts current in only one direction. When AC voltage drives a diode forward, current flows. When the AC reverses, the diode blocks. This selective conduction is what turns alternating current into pulsating direct current.

 Three circuit configurations use this property: the half wave rectifier , the centre tap full wave rectifier , and the bridge rectifier . Each trades circuit complexity for better DC output. Click any term to expand.

 Half Wave Rectifier: One diode in series with the load. Only the positive half cycle of the AC passes to the output. The negative half cycle is blocked. Output is pulsating DC at the supply frequency. Average output = 0.318 × Vpeak. Efficiency is low (40.6%) because half the input is wasted. Suitable for low-power applications where simplicity matters more than efficiency.

 Centre Tap Full Wave Rectifier: Two diodes and a centre tapped transformer. During the positive half cycle, D1 conducts. During the negative half cycle, D2 conducts. Both half cycles appear at the output in the same polarity. Average output = 0.636 × Vpeak. Ripple frequency is twice the supply frequency. Requires a centre tapped transformer, which adds cost and size.

 Bridge Rectifier: Four diodes in a bridge arrangement. No centre tapped transformer needed. During the positive half cycle, D1 and D3 conduct. During the negative half cycle, D2 and D4 conduct. Both half cycles drive current through the load in the same direction. Average output = 0.636 × Vpeak (minus two diode drops). The most widely used diode rectifier circuit in modern power supplies.




 

 
 0.318 × Vp
 Average DC output of a half wave diode rectifier circuit


 0.636 × Vp
 Average DC output of a full wave diode rectifier circuit


 40.6%
 Efficiency of a half wave rectifier -- full wave gives 81.2%


 4 diodes
 Bridge rectifier uses four diodes -- most common configuration in use today

 Three Diode Rectifier Circuit Types


 1. Half Wave Rectifier


 The simplest diode rectifier circuit uses one diode in series with the load. During the positive half cycle, the diode conducts; during the negative half, it blocks and output is zero.

 Only half the available AC power reaches the load.


 
 Half Wave Rectifier Output

 Vdc = Vpeak / π = 0.318 × Vpeak

 
 Vdc : average DC output voltage

 Vpeak : peak value of the AC input (Vrms × √2)

 Vrms : RMS supply voltage (e.g. 230 V from mains)

 Efficiency : 40.6% -- less than half the input power reaches the load

 Ripple frequency : equals the supply frequency (50 Hz or 60 Hz)
 




 The output has large gaps at mains frequency. A smoothing capacitor reduces ripple but a half wave diode rectifier needs a much larger capacitor than a full wave design for equivalent ripple.

 See the capacitor types guide for electrolytic capacitor selection.

 
 
 
 2. Full Wave Centre Tap Rectifier


 Two diodes and a centre tapped transformer. The centre tap is connected to the negative output terminal (ground). Each diode conducts on alternate half cycles, so both halves of the AC waveform appear at the output.


 
 Full Wave Centre Tap Output

 Vdc = 2 × Vpeak / π = 0.636 × Vpeak

 
 Vdc : average DC output voltage

 Vpeak : peak voltage of each transformer half-secondary

 Efficiency : 81.2% -- both half cycles used

 Ripple frequency : 2 × supply frequency (100 Hz for 50 Hz mains)

 Limitation : each half of the secondary only delivers half the transformer secondary voltage to the load
 




 The centre tap doubles ripple to 100 Hz, improving smoothing. Each diode must withstand the full secondary voltage in reverse -- a key limitation.


 3. Full Wave Bridge Rectifier


 Four diodes in a bridge arrangement. No centre tapped transformer required. During the positive half cycle, D1 and D3 conduct; during the negative half cycle, D2 and D4 conduct. In both cases, current flows through the load in the same direction.


 
 Bridge Rectifier Output

 Vdc = 0.636 × Vpeak − 2 × VF

 
 Vdc : average DC output voltage

 Vpeak : peak secondary voltage of the transformer

 VF : forward voltage drop per diode (typically 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for Schottky)

 Two diodes conduct simultaneously, so subtract 2 × VF from the output

 Ripple frequency : 2 × supply frequency (100 Hz for 50 Hz mains)

 Efficiency : 81.2% (same as centre tap, but with two-diode voltage drop)
 




 At high currents, the two-diode forward voltage drop in the bridge rectifier (typically 1.4 V for silicon diodes) becomes significant. At 5 V output from a 5 A supply, 7 W is lost in the diodes alone. For efficiency critical designs, Schottky diodes (0.3 V forward vol
